segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Take care not to practice your righteousness in front of people in order to be seen by them; otherwise you have no reward with your Father who is in the heavens.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “So when you give to the needy, do not sound a trumpet ahead of you, as the performers do in the synagogues and in the streets, so that they may be honored by people. Truly I tell you, they have been paid their reward in full.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But when you give to the needy, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: so that your giving may be in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “And when you pray, you are not to be like the performers; for they love to pray standing in the synagogues and on the corners of the main streets, so that they may be seen by people. Truly I tell you, they have been paid their reward in full.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But you, when you pray, go into your inner room, shut your door, and pray to your Father who is in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “And when you pray, do not babble on as the Gentiles do, for they think that they will be heard because of their many words.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So do not be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask him.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You, then, are to pray like this: ‘Our Father in the heavens, may your name be held holy,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: may your kingdom come, may your will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Give us today our daily bread,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and do not bring us into testing, but rescue us from the evil one.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “For if you forgive people their offenses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: but if you do not forgive people, neither will your Father forgive your offenses.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “And when you fast, do not put on a gloomy look as the performers do, for they make their faces unsightly so that they may be seen by people to be fasting. Truly I tell you, they have been paid their reward in full.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But you, when you fast, put oil on your head and wash your face,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: so that your fasting may be seen not by people but by your Father who is in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and decay destroy and where thieves break in and steal;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: but store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor decay destroys and where thieves do not break in or steal.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “The lamp of the body is the eye. So if your eye is generous, your whole body will be full of light;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: but if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness. If, then, the light within you is darkness, how great that darkness is!

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “No one can be a slave to two masters; for they will either hate the one and love the other, or be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot be a slave to both God and wealth.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “For this reason I tell you: do not worry about your life, what you will eat, or about your body, what you will put on. Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothing?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Look at the birds of the sky: they do not sow or reap or gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not worth far more than they are?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And which of you by worrying can add a single cubit to your span of life?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And why do you worry about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they do not toil or spin.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Yet I tell you that not even Solomon in all his glory was dressed like one of these.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But if this is how God clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, will he not much more clothe you, you of little faith?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So do not worry, saying, ‘What are we to eat?’ or ‘What are we to drink?’ or ‘What are we to wear?’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For the Gentiles seek after all these things, and your heavenly Father knows that you need them all.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But seek first his kingdom and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself. The day’s own trouble is enough for the day.

notes.note: Here the word means concrete acts of religious duty; the three examples that follow are giving to the needy, prayer and fasting. Greek has one word-family where English has two (righteous/just, righteousness/justice), so the same word elsewhere comes close to “justice”. Some later manuscripts read “almsgiving” in this verse, which lies behind the King James “alms”.

The Greek is plural, a Semitic turn of phrase that Matthew uses often for God’s dwelling. Most translations flatten it to “heaven”. The plural is kept here wherever the Greek has it; the singular in verses 10 and 20 is rendered “heaven”.

The Greek word, the source of English “hypocrite”, was the ordinary term for a stage actor, though in Jewish Greek before the New Testament it had already come to mean a godless or insincere person, and most translations keep “hypocrites”. In this chapter the picture of playing to an audience is alive in the context (trumpets, street corners, being seen), so “performers” is used in verses 2, 5 and 16. Elsewhere this translation keeps “hypocrites”.

notes.phrase: they have been paid their reward in full
notes.note: The verb is the standard term on surviving receipts of the period for payment received in full, so the saying has a commercial ring: the account is settled and nothing more is owed. Many modern translations similarly have “they have received their reward in full”.

notes.phrase: may your name be held holy
notes.note: The verb is built on the ordinary Greek word for “holy”. God’s name cannot be made holy, so the sense is that it be treated and acknowledged as holy; the passive may also imply a request that God himself bring this about. “Hallowed” says the same thing in English that is no longer current.

The meaning of this Greek word is not known. It is almost unattested outside the Lord’s Prayer, and ancient interpreters already disagreed about it. The main proposals are “for the coming day”, “necessary for existence” and “for today”; with no secure alternative, the traditional “daily” is kept.

In the usage of the period the word mainly means a putting to the proof, an ordeal that shows whether someone will stay faithful; it can also mean enticement to sin. Most English versions keep “temptation” here, and some have “time of trial”. Scholars disagree about which sense is in view, so “testing” is an editorial choice; it avoids the suggestion that God lures people into wrongdoing.

The Greek form can be masculine (“the evil one”, meaning the devil) or neuter (“evil”). The traditional English prayer has “deliver us from evil”. Many modern translations and commentators prefer “the evil one”, since Matthew uses the expression elsewhere for the devil (13:19, 38), but either reading is possible.

notes.phrase: rescue us from the evil one
notes.traditional: For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory forever. Amen.
notes.note: The familiar closing words, “For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory forever. Amen,” are absent from the earliest manuscripts and are not in the Greek text translated here. They appear, in varying forms, in most later manuscripts and are generally regarded as an early addition made for use in worship.

The word means a wrongful act against God or another person. “Trespasses” is traditional, but in current English that word chiefly suggests entering property without permission. It is a different Greek word from the “debts” of verse 12, where debt is a figure for sin.

The Greek word means “eating” or “consuming”. “Rust” is the traditional rendering, but this is not the usual Greek word for rust, and it may instead refer to insects or vermin that eat stored goods. “Decay” leaves the kind of consuming open.

The Greek word means “single” or “sound”, and most translations have “healthy”, keeping the physical picture of an eye that lets light in. But the “evil eye” of the next verse is a known Jewish idiom for stinginess, related words are used of generous giving, and the saying sits between treasure in heaven and slavery to wealth. “Generous” follows that context, at the cost of the physical image.

The verb is the one for a slave’s service, not for paid employment. The saying depends on this: a hired worker can have two employers, but a slave is owned and is wholly at one master’s disposal. Most translations have “serve”.

The Greek keeps an Aramaic word, mamona, meaning wealth or property, which the King James Version carried over as “mammon”. It is not the name of a god; the saying treats wealth as if it were a rival master. Most modern translations have “wealth” or “money”.

notes.traditional: what you will eat or what you will drink
notes.note: Many manuscripts add “or what you will drink” here, and most English versions include it. The Greek text translated here does not have the words; they may have been added to match verse 31.

notes.phrase: a single cubit to your span of life
notes.traditional: add one cubit unto his stature
notes.note: The Greek noun can mean either age (length of life) or height, and a cubit is a measure of length, about half a meter. “Stature” is the older rendering, but half a meter of extra height would be no small thing, and the saying calls for something trivial. Most modern translations therefore take it as a short stretch added to one’s life.

notes.traditional: the kingdom of God and his righteousness
notes.note: Many manuscripts read “the kingdom of God and his righteousness”, which is the familiar wording. The Greek text translated here has only “the kingdom and his righteousness”; “his” refers to the heavenly Father of verse 32 and is taken here with both nouns.

candidates.reason: Recurs across the Gospels and Paul, where versions waver between “serve” and “be a slave to”, and the choice should match whatever is decided for δοῦλος.
An Aramaic word left untranslated in the Greek, occurring only here and three times in Luke 16; a single decision is needed between “wealth”, “money” and the loanword “Mammon”.
Translators split between “worry” and “be anxious”, and the verb and its noun recur in Luke 10 and 12, 1 Corinthians 7 and Philippians 4, where the positive sense “be concerned for” also appears.
The traditional “alms” is archaic and the word recurs in Luke and Acts, so one modern equivalent should be fixed (charitable giving, gifts to the poor, acts of mercy).
Versions vary between “Gentiles” and “pagans” here and at Matthew 5:47 and 18:17, and the rendering needs coordinating with the register entry for ἔθνος.
